Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo

October 29, 2026
Abstract

The local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) of the homogeneous electron gas describes how exchange and correlation modify the response to a static perturbation, and enters dielectric screening, effective electron–electron interactions, and the exchange-correlation kernel of time-dependent density functional theory. Accurate zero-temperature data for G⁡(q)G(q), however, remain limited to metallic densities, rs≤10r_{s}\leq 10. In this work, we present diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density-density response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and of G⁡(q)G(q) for 2≤rs≤1002\leq r_{s}\leq 100, and describe and discuss the methodological steps that enabled these calculations. We show how optimization of the perturbing potential in the trial wave function has an important effect, as a poor choice can reverse the sign of the response. A closed-form expression is provided for its optimal value, together with the density dependence of the linear-response window. We further show that backflow correlations leave χ⁡(q)\chi(q) unchanged and that G⁡(q)G(q) depends only weakly on system size even at very low density, so that Slater–Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes suffice. Together, these results provide a practical guide for future quantum Monte Carlo calculations of response properties of the electron gas and real materials. Our results agree with previous diffusion Monte Carlo data at metallic densities for q>kFq>k_{F}, and extend them below kFk_{F}. They also agree with diagrammatic quantum Monte Carlo at rs=2r_{s}=2. At lower densities, our results show that G⁡(q)G(q) develops a nonmonotonic structure at intermediate wave vectors, where the response approaches that of the noninteracting gas. Quantitative agreement is seen with finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo data, suggesting that the previously reported finite-temperature structure is inherited from the ground state. Using a parametrization of G⁡(q)G(q) that reproduces our data throughout the liquid phase, we relate this structure to short-range order in the pair correlation function and the static structure factor.

I Introduction

The response properties of the homogeneous electron gas (HEG) have been of considerable theoretical interest for over half a century [1, 2, 3, 4]. They describe how the gas rearranges in response to an external potential of a given wavelength [5]. For a static external potential, this information is contained in the static linear density response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q), and the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) isolates the part of it due to exchange and correlation [3]. Both enter directly into descriptions of dielectric screening [6], effective electron–electron interactions [7, 8], and the exchange-correlation (xc) kernel of time-dependent density functional theory [9]. Early studies of the static response were based on analytical and diagrammatic schemes that satisfied the compressibility sum rule and the large-qq limit [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 1, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 6, 25, 26, 27, 28, 3].

The first quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) calculations of the static response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) of the gas at zero temperature were carried out in parallel by two groups in 1992. Sugiyama, Bowen, and Alder demonstrated the approach on the charged Bose gas [29], while Moroni, Ceperley, and Senatore applied it to the two-dimensional electron gas and liquid 4He [30]. The first application to the three-dimensional electron gas was made by Bowen et al. [31], using variational Monte Carlo, fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC), and released-node Green’s function Monte Carlo to confirm that the fixed-node results are exact within statistical error bars. The definitive zero-temperature results were later provided by Moroni, Ceperley, and Senatore in their benchmark study [32], which yielded accurate DMC data for χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and G⁡(q)G(q) across the metallic density range rs=2r_{s}=2–1010, alongside an analytical interpolation of G⁡(q)G(q) that satisfies the known asymptotic limits. Their data, calculated by adding an external perturbation to the Hamiltonian, showed that G⁡(q)G(q) varies smoothly between these limits with a crossover near 2​kF2k_{F}. These calculations have served as the primary benchmark for describing exchange-correlation effects in materials for nearly three decades.

At finite temperature, there have been significant efforts especially using the path integral Monte Carlo (PIMC) approach. Dornheim et al. have computed χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and G⁡(q)G(q) for the strongly coupled, i.e., low-density, electron liquid at reduced temperatures Θ=T/TF=0.5\Theta=T/T_{F}=0.5–44 for a wide range of rsr_{s} values including rs=20r_{s}=20, rs=50r_{s}=50, 100100, and 200200 via imaginary-time correlation functions [33, 34, 35, 36]. Their findings show indications of structure in G⁡(q)G(q) at intermediate wave vectors; however, with thermal and correlation effects inextricably entangled at finite TT, a clear origin of this feature could not be established.

Following the calculations of Moroni et al., several efforts to parametrize G⁡(q)G(q) have been made. Corradini et al. fitted an analytical form to the Moroni et al. data [37], which made fxc​(q)f_{\mathrm{xc}}(q) conveniently available for use in ab initio calculations. This parametrization has been widely adopted ever since [38, 39, 40, 9, 41, 35, 42]. More recently, Kukkonen and Chen provided new results for G⁡(q)G(q) at rs=1r_{s}=1 and rs=2r_{s}=2 using diagrammatic QMC [8]. These results (along with the Moroni et al. data) were then used by Kaplan and Kukkonen to construct an improved parametrization [43].

Crucially, despite these efforts on parametrizing G⁡(q)G(q), the underlying QMC data for the unpolarized gas do not extend beyond rs=10r_{s}=10. Two distinct factors have obstructed the extension of the perturbative DMC approach of Moroni et al. to lower densities. The first is cost. Each point of a χ⁡(q)\chi(q) curve requires DMC calculations at several perturbation amplitudes, each preceded by an independent optimization of the trial wave function, which converges more slowly as the density decreases; a single curve at a single density can easily amount to ∼103\sim\!10^{3} separate QMC calculations. This cost is met by modern implementations and computing resources [44, 45], which were instrumental for the present work. The second factor is not relieved by computing resources: several systematic errors that are controlled at metallic densities remain uncharacterized at rs≳10r_{s}\gtrsim 10. The usable range of perturbation strength to ensure linear response has not been established, which increases computational cost if one must repeat calculations at each density and several perturbation strengths to verify the validity of linear response. The effect of the nodal surface of the trial wave function on the extracted χ⁡(q)\chi(q) has not been tested, and the finite-size effects in χ⁡(q)\chi(q) have not been investigated at large rsr_{s}.

In this work, we present DMC calculations of the static response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) of the three-dimensional electron gas at zero temperature, covering the entire liquid phase up to rs=100r_{s}=100. The physical implications of this new regime are discussed in a companion paper [46], where we show the emergence of a nonmonotonic structure in G⁡(q)G(q) at intermediate wave vectors and how it manifests as short-range order in the electron liquid, together with a new parametrization of G⁡(q)G(q) that can be used for many-body calculations. In this paper, we focus on the methodology that made those findings possible, addressing in turn each of the obstacles above. We determine the optimal variational parameters of the trial wave function and reduce them to a closed form valid across the whole density range, so that the optimization does not have to be repeated for every calculation; we establish how far the perturbation amplitude can be increased while remaining within the linear response regime as the density decreases; we examine whether more sophisticated forms of the trial wave function meaningfully alter the extracted susceptibility, and we investigate the finite-size effects at low density.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II gives a complete description of the methodology, including how the response function is extracted, how the regime of linear response is determined, how the trial wave function is constructed and optimized, how finite-size and time-step errors are treated, and how G⁡(q)G(q) is parametrized. Section III presents the results for χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and G⁡(q)G(q) for rs=2r_{s}=2–100100 and highlights the features that emerge at large rsr_{s}. Subsection III.2 relates these features to the structure of the strongly coupled electron liquid, as seen in its pair correlation function and static structure factor, and to its evolution toward the Wigner crystal. We conclude in Sec. IV.

II Method

II.1 Static response from a cosine perturbation

We extract the response properties by subjecting an otherwise homogeneous electron gas to a weak static cosine perturbation,

vext​(𝐫)=2​v𝐪​cos⁡(𝐪⋅𝐫),v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})=2v_{\mathbf{q}}\cos(\mathbf q\!\cdot\!\mathbf r), (1)

where v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} is the amplitude of the perturbation. The response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) can then be extracted by expanding the perturbed energy (per particle) in powers of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}. Within linear response, the ground-state energy is

E⁡(v𝐪)=E0+χ⁡(q)n0​v𝐪2+⋯,E(v_{\mathbf{q}})=E_{0}+\frac{\chi(q)}{n_{0}}v^{2}_{\mathbf{q}}+\cdots, (2)

where E0E_{0} is the unperturbed ground-state energy per particle (i.e., v𝐪=0v_{\mathbf{q}}=0), and χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is the static density-density response function. Higher-order terms carry information about the higher-order response, which we do not explore in this work. By fitting the energy to this form, one can extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q) from the coefficient of the quadratic term.

A crucial quantity that can be obtained directly from χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q), which encodes the exchange and correlation effects beyond the random-phase approximation (RPA). It is defined via the Dyson equation,

G⁡(q)=−fxc​(q)vc​(q)=1+χ−1​(q)−χ0−1​(q)vc​(q),G(q)=-\frac{f_{\mathrm{xc}}(q)}{v_{c}(q)}=1+\frac{\chi^{-1}(q)-\chi^{-1}_{0}(q)}{v_{c}(q)}, (3)

where fxc​(q)f_{\mathrm{xc}}(q) is the exchange-correlation kernel, vc​(q)=4​π/q2v_{c}(q)=4\pi/q^{2} is the Coulomb interaction, and χ0​(q)\chi_{0}(q) is the static response function of the noninteracting system [3]. The noninteracting and RPA limits are reached by setting G⁡(q)=1G(q)=1 and G⁡(q)=0G(q)=0, respectively. Since χ⁡(q)\chi(q) will be obtained from stochastic estimates of the energy E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}), it carries a statistical error, which propagates into G⁡(q)G(q) with a prefactor proportional to (q/χ⁡(q))2\left(q/\chi(q)\right)^{2} that inevitably diverges in both the low- and high-qq limits. However, this is of no practical concern since G⁡(q)G(q) is known analytically in both limits [25]. The low-qq limit of the local field factor is given by limq→0G⁡(q)=A​(q/kF)2\lim_{q\to 0}G(q)=A(q/k_{F})^{2} whereas the high-qq limit is given by limq→∞G⁡(q)=C​(q/kF)2+B\lim_{q\to\infty}G(q)=C(q/k_{F})^{2}+B. All quantities A,B,CA,B,C are known expressions and parametrizations as a function of rsr_{s} [32, 37, 26, 25]. We provide the explicit expressions for A⁡(rs)A(r_{s}), B⁡(rs)B(r_{s}), and C⁡(rs)C(r_{s}) in Appendix A.

To compute the perturbed energies E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}), we employ the state-of-the-art fixed-node DMC method [47, 48, 32], implemented in QMCPACK [44, 45]. DMC is the gold standard for computing ground-state properties of quantum many-body systems, and it has been extensively used as a benchmark for the homogeneous electron gas [48, 49]. Modifications were made to include the cosine perturbation to the Hamiltonian. Once E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) is obtained, χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is extracted from the energy by performing a least-squares fitting procedure to the form of Eq. (2). The procedure is summarized in Fig. 1 for two different densities, rs=5r_{s}=5 and rs=70r_{s}=70, and for three different wave vectors. We carefully select the range of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} used to fit E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) and extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q) so that it remains in the linear-response regime, where the signal-to-noise ratio is high. The resulting maximum perturbation is parametrized by the fit v𝐪max=0.1212​rs−1.43v_{\mathbf{q}}^{\mathrm{max}}=0.1212\,r_{s}^{-1.43} Ha, where the exponent is determined by the noninteracting problem and the prefactor is fitted to QMC data. More details of this selection process can be found in Appendix B.

II.2 Trial wave function

We construct our trial wave function using both Slater–Jastrow (SJ) and Slater–Jastrow-backflow (SJ-BF) forms [50, 51, 52, 53, 54]. The former is the standard form used in many QMC calculations in which the nodal surface is fixed by the Slater determinant of single-particle orbitals, while the latter allows for modifications of the single-particle coordinates in the Slater determinant by introducing a displacement for the jjth electron, which depends on the positions of all other electrons. Such a transformation introduces additional variational parameters that can be optimized to further minimize the energy. To compare both forms and verify that our choice of trial wave function does not bias the extraction of χ⁡(q)\chi(q), we performed a subset of calculations with and without a backflow transformation. We find that while the backflow transformation significantly improves the energies obtained from DMC, it does not affect the extraction of χ⁡(q)\chi(q), which is related to the curvature of the energy with respect to the perturbation amplitude v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}, and not the absolute value of the energy itself. Figure 1 demonstrates this point for (a) rs=5r_{s}=5 with Ne=162N_{e}=162, and for (b) rs=70r_{s}=70 with Ne=38N_{e}=38, at three wave vectors. The resulting χ⁡(q)\chi(q) values obtained with and without backflow transformation are in agreement within error bars, even though the energies themselves are significantly different. Thus, throughout this work, we will mainly use the Slater–Jastrow trial wave function without backflow transformation (unless stated otherwise) to extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q), which is computationally more efficient and shown not to bias our results. The SJ trial wave function is constructed as ΨT​(𝐑)=eJ⁡(𝐑)​det⁡[ϕi​(𝐫j)]\Psi_{T}(\mathbf{R})=e^{J(\mathbf{R})}\det[\phi_{i}(\mathbf{r}_{j})], where J⁡(𝐑)J(\mathbf{R}) is the Jastrow factor that captures electron-electron correlations, and det⁡[ϕi​(𝐫j)]\det[\phi_{i}(\mathbf{r}_{j})] is the Slater determinant of noninteracting single-particle wave functions. For the latter, we will use the one of noninteracting single-electrons [55] perturbed by an effective external potential of the same form,

vexteff​(𝐫)=α​vext​(𝐫).v^{\mathrm{eff}}_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r})=\alpha v_{\mathrm{ext}}(\mathbf{r}). (4)

By construction, vexteffv_{\mathrm{ext}}^{\mathrm{eff}} does not have to be equal to the amplitude of the external potential v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}, so α\alpha must be treated as a variational parameter that yields the minimum energy. Therefore, the optimization is to be achieved in two steps. First, one performs variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculations to minimize the energy computed from the Hamiltonian perturbed by Eq. (1), with respect to the parameters in the Jastrow factor, for a given α\alpha in Eq. (4). This procedure is then repeated for different α\alpha values to obtain the VMC energy as a function of α\alpha, i.e., Ev​(α)E^{v}(\alpha), and extract the optimal α\alpha. In this work, we find that the α\alpha that minimizes the variational energy is different for each value of 𝐪\mathbf{q} and rsr_{s} and needs to be optimized for each case separately. We emphasize that the α\alpha-optimization is crucial to obtain reliable results for χ⁡(q)\chi(q) for all rsr_{s} values. This is demonstrated in Fig. 2(a) for rs=50r_{s}=50 and q=1.2​kFq=1.2k_{F}. A poorly chosen α\alpha changes not only the energy but also the curvature of E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}), whose sign can even be reversed, and gives rise to an unphysical χ⁡(q)>0\chi(q)>0. As α\alpha is reduced (for this particular wave vector and density), the curvature of E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) converges to a stable value, and yields the correct χ⁡(q)\chi(q) at α≃0.15\alpha\simeq 0.15. Figure 2(b) shows that the variance of the local energy decreases accordingly as α\alpha approaches the optimal value, i.e., the minimum of Ev​(α)E^{v}(\alpha) (vertical dashed line). Performing over 700700 VMC calculations using the above approach, we found that the optimal α\alpha is reproduced by the following form for rs=2r_{s}=2–100100:

α⁡(q,rs)=1−e−α0​(rs)​(q/kF)α1​(rs),\alpha(q,r_{s})=1-e^{-\alpha_{0}(r_{s})\,(q/k_{F})^{\alpha_{1}(r_{s})}}, (5)

where α0​(rs)=0.7276​rs−0.6050\alpha_{0}(r_{s})=0.7276\,r_{s}^{-0.6050} and α1​(rs)=1.1603​rs0.3513\alpha_{1}(r_{s})=1.1603\,r_{s}^{0.3513}. Figure 2(c) shows α⁡(q,rs)\alpha(q,r_{s}) as a function of q/kFq/k_{F} for six different values of rsr_{s}. Once the optimal α\alpha is obtained, we perform DMC calculations to obtain the perturbed energies E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}), which are then used to extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q).

II.3 Size effects and time-step error

It has been shown that the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) is much less sensitive to finite-size effects than the energy [32] for rs≤10r_{s}\leq 10. This is due to the fact that exchange and correlation effects are short-ranged. Therefore, one can assume G⁡(𝐪,N)≃G⁡(q,∞)G(\mathbf{q},N)\simeq G(q,\infty) to mitigate finite-size effects in our calculations as follows

χ−1​(𝐪,∞)=χ−1​(𝐪,N)+Δ​χ0−1​(𝐪),\chi^{-1}(\mathbf{q},\infty)=\chi^{-1}(\mathbf{q},N)+\Delta\chi^{-1}_{0}(\mathbf{q}), (6)

where Δ​χ0−1​(𝐪)=χ0−1​(𝐪,∞)−χ0−1​(𝐪,N)\Delta\chi_{0}^{-1}(\mathbf{q})=\chi_{0}^{-1}(\mathbf{q},\infty)-\chi_{0}^{-1}(\mathbf{q},N) represents the finite-size correction in the noninteracting response function. Throughout this work, we use Eq. (6) to correct the finite-size effects in χ⁡(q)\chi(q). At low-rsr_{s} values, Eq. (6) is known to hold quite well [32]. However, at high-rsr_{s} values, such a claim is questionable and merits further investigation.

In this subsection, we investigate the validity of this hypothesis at large rsr_{s} by testing two finite-size features of the Fermi sphere: its resolution, set by NeN_{e}, and its isotropy at fixed NeN_{e}. Figure 3(a) shows the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) at rs=50r_{s}=50 for different system sizes: Ne=38N_{e}=38 (squares), Ne=54N_{e}=54 (triangles), and Ne=162N_{e}=162 (circles). The inset zooms into the region around 2​kF2k_{F}. Overall, the DMC data points for different system sizes collapse onto a single curve, confirming the insensitivity of G⁡(q)G(q) to finite-size effects, even at large rsr_{s} values. Although the statistical uncertainty of G⁡(q)G(q) at q>4​kFq>4k_{F} and q≲1.6​kFq\lesssim 1.6\,k_{F} is too large to resolve differences between system sizes, both the small- and large-qq limits are analytically known (given in Appendix A). Figure 3(b) shows the difference between two χ⁡(q)\chi(q)-values that have the same |𝐪||\mathbf{q}| but different directions, i.e., δ​χ𝐪^=χ⁡(𝐪=(2,2,1)​2​πL)−χ⁡(𝐪=(3,0,0)​2​πL)\delta\chi_{\hat{\mathbf{q}}}=\chi\left(\mathbf{q}=(2,2,1)\frac{2\pi}{L}\right)-\chi\left(\mathbf{q}=(3,0,0)\frac{2\pi}{L}\right) as a function of rsr_{s}. Since in the thermodynamic limit, δ​χ𝐪^\delta\chi_{\hat{\mathbf{q}}} should vanish, any nonzero value of δ​χ𝐪^\delta\chi_{\hat{\mathbf{q}}} indicates the presence of finite-size effects. This is shown by the triangles in Fig. 3(b), which correspond to the raw χ⁡(q)\chi(q) values. If Eq. (6) captures the dominant finite-size error, the corrected χ⁡(q)\chi(q) should give δ​χ𝐪^=0\delta\chi_{\hat{\mathbf{q}}}=0. This is shown by the circles in Fig. 3(b), where the difference is effectively reduced to zero within error bars. The anisotropy of χ⁡(𝐪,N)\chi(\mathbf{q},N) at fixed NeN_{e} is therefore entirely due to χ0​(𝐪,N)\chi_{0}(\mathbf{q},N), and it is removed by the correction in Eq. (6).

The remaining question is how large this correction is, and how it changes with increasing coupling. For this, we show in Fig. 4(a) the finite-size correction to the static response, Δ​χ≡χ⁡(q,∞)−χ⁡(𝐪,N)\Delta\chi\equiv\chi(q,\infty)-\chi(\mathbf{q},N), obtained from Eq. (6) and given in units of NF=kF/π2N_{F}=k_{F}/\pi^{2}. For all densities, Δ​χ\Delta\chi is localized in qq and vanishes at small and large qq. The correction is largest at high density around q≃1.5​kFq\simeq 1.5k_{F}, and it becomes smaller at low density, where it shifts to q≃2​kFq\simeq 2k_{F}. It is predominantly negative, i.e., the finite system underestimates |χ⁡(q)||\chi(q)| where the correction is largest, and its magnitude always remains below 0.1​NF0.1N_{F} (where NF=−χ0​(q→0)N_{F}=-\chi_{0}(q\to 0) sets the natural scale of the response). Its root-mean-square [Fig. 4(b)] over all computed wave vectors decreases from ≈4×10−2\approx 4\times 10^{-2} at rs=2r_{s}=2 to ≈1×10−2\approx 1\times 10^{-2} at rs≳70r_{s}\gtrsim 70 for Ne=162N_{e}=162, and approaches the typical statistical uncertainty of χ⁡(q)\chi(q) (around 0.5×10−20.5\times 10^{-2} at rs=90r_{s}=90). Ne=54N_{e}=54 shows the same decreasing trend. The finite-size correction to χ⁡(q)\chi(q) from Eq. (6) is therefore modest at all densities, and it decreases further as the coupling increases. Twist averaging is an alternative route to removing one-body finite-size errors, but is more expensive, since it requires an independent calculation for each twist. In Appendix C, we show that at fixed NeN_{e} (canonical twist averaging), it approaches our corrected results to within 2–3%, with a small residual bias due to keeping the number of electrons fixed.

Besides finite-size effects, the DMC energies carry a time-step error. Since χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is extracted from small energy differences between perturbed states, any time-step bias that depends on qq or v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} would directly bias the curvature of E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}). Figure 5 therefore shows the time-step extrapolation for the perturbed gas at two wave vectors and two densities. The DMC energies exhibit a linear dependence on the time step τ\tau as it approaches zero. For rs=5r_{s}=5, the energy is converged within error bars for τ≤0.5\tau\leq 0.5 Ha-1, while for rs=70r_{s}=70, the energy is converged for τ≤14\tau\leq 14 Ha-1. This is consistent with the fact that for such a large rsr_{s} value, the system is in a strongly correlated regime where the energy scales shrink, and the DMC algorithm can take larger time steps without losing accuracy. In our production runs, we have used τ=rs/40\tau=r_{s}/40 Ha-1 (vertical dashed lines), which is well within the converged regime for all rsr_{s} values considered in this work.

II.4 Analytical fit

All solid curves labeled “This work” that we will present in Sec. III are obtained from a single parametrization of G⁡(q)G(q), introduced in the companion paper [46]. It interpolates between a low- and a high-rsr_{s} form,

G⁡(q)=(1−s)​Glo​(q)+s​Ghi​(q),s=tanh⁡(rs4/250),G(q)=(1-s)\,G_{\mathrm{lo}}(q)+s\,G_{\mathrm{hi}}(q),\quad s=\tanh\!\left(r_{s}^{4}/250\right), (7)

where both terms take the form of Kaplan and Kukkonen [43],

Glo,hi​(q)=A​x2​h⏟small ​x+θ​xn+2​h⏟interm. ​x+(C​x2+B)​(1−h)⏟large ​x,G_{\mathrm{lo,hi}}(q)=\underbrace{Ax^{2}h}_{\text{small }x}+\underbrace{\theta x^{n+2}h}_{\text{interm. }x}+\underbrace{(Cx^{2}+B)(1-h)}_{\text{large }x}, (8)

with x=q/kFx=q/k_{F}, the exact coefficients AA, BB, and CC given in Appendix A, and the crossover function

h=ea3​a4−1ea3​x4/16+ea3​a4−2.h=\frac{e^{a_{3}a_{4}}-1}{e^{a_{3}x^{4}/16}+e^{a_{3}a_{4}}-2}. (9)

The function hh decays from 11 to 00, with position set by a4a_{4} and width by a3a_{3}. Since h→1h\to 1 for x→0x\to 0 and the intermediate term vanishes faster than x2x^{2} for n>0n>0, Eq. (8) satisfies the compressibility sum rule and the large-qq limit exactly, at every rsr_{s}. The low-rsr_{s} form Glo​(q)G_{\mathrm{lo}}(q) is the original parametrization of Ref. [43], with n=4n=4 and θ=a0+a1​e−a2​rs\theta=a_{0}+a_{1}e^{-a_{2}r_{s}}. Kaplan and Kukkonen reported a0a_{0} and a2a_{2} with sizable uncertainties, due to the growing error bars of the diagrammatic QMC data above 2​kF2k_{F} [see orange shaded area in Fig. 6(d)]. Refitting these two parameters to include our DMC data, we obtain a0=−0.0046277a_{0}=-0.0046277, within the original error bar, and a2=0.622624a_{2}=0.622624, at the edge of the original uncertainty, and keep the remaining parameters at their published values, a1=0.0155766a_{1}=0.0155766, a3=3.516054a_{3}=3.516054, and a4=1.015830a_{4}=1.015830.

The high-rsr_{s} form Ghi​(q)G_{\mathrm{hi}}(q) keeps the same structure, but lets the exponent evolve with density, n=a5′+a6′​e−a7′​rsn=a^{\prime}_{5}+a^{\prime}_{6}e^{-a^{\prime}_{7}r_{s}}, while θ=a0′+a1′​e−a2′​rs\theta=a^{\prime}_{0}+a^{\prime}_{1}e^{-a^{\prime}_{2}r_{s}} keeps the original form with refitted parameters. The crossover hh is moved to larger xx through a4′a^{\prime}_{4}, with a broader width a3′a^{\prime}_{3}. At large rsr_{s}, θ\theta becomes negative, and the intermediate term allows for a possible nonmonotonic behavior of G⁡(q)G(q), which we will discuss in Sec. III. The values of the primed parameters are given in Ref. [46]. The switching function ss is negligible at rs=1r_{s}=1, reaches s≃0.06s\simeq 0.06 at rs=2r_{s}=2, and is close to unity for rs≥5r_{s}\geq 5, so that Glo​(q)G_{\mathrm{lo}}(q) is recovered in the regime of metallic densities, and Ghi​(q)G_{\mathrm{hi}}(q) describes the strongly coupled regime.

III Results

We have performed DMC calculations for the unpolarized three-dimensional electron gas between 2≤rs≤1002\leq r_{s}\leq 100, with Ne=38N_{e}=38, 54, and 162 electrons. The values of rsr_{s} are chosen to cover the entire liquid phase of the electron gas, and perhaps even beyond the Wigner crystallization transition, since current estimates for the transition vary between rs≃87r_{s}\simeq 87 and rs≃113r_{s}\simeq 113 [56, 48, 57, 58]. Note, however, that our ansatz is limited to represent the liquid phase only, even if it is metastable. Our results are compared to the existing Corradini et al. parametrization, which becomes an extrapolation at rs>10r_{s}>10, in order to highlight new features emerging in the strongly coupled regime.

III.1 Static response function and local field factor from DMC

We present our results for the static density response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q), using Eq. (3), for rs=2,5,10r_{s}=2,5,10 in the upper and lower panels of Fig. 6, respectively. The DMC data are shown as circles, while the dash-dotted curve is the analytical parametrization of Ref. [37] designed specifically for these rsr_{s} values to fit the data from Ref. [32]. As a first demonstration, our results for χ⁡(q)\chi(q) are in excellent agreement with the existing parametrizations fitted at these same densities. The response of the system vanishes as q→0q\to 0 quadratically (governed by the compressibility limit) due to the long-range nature of the Coulomb interaction, and peaks at q≃2​kFq\simeq 2k_{F} before approaching the RPA limit at large qq. The peak becomes more pronounced with decreasing density, while its departure from RPA is an indication of growing exchange-correlation effects. Importantly, our simulations provide the first DMC data for q<kFq<k_{F}, and they are consistent with the compressibility limit. This is important for numerous applications [8, 43, 59, 60, 61].

On the other hand, the case of G⁡(q)G(q) is more delicate, as it isolates the exchange-correlation contribution that may not be immediately apparent in χ⁡(q)\chi(q). We show G⁡(q)G(q) in Figs. 6(d)–(f), where the small- and large-qq limits are given as gray dashed lines. For rs=2r_{s}=2, we present additional data (orange shaded region) obtained from diagrammatic QMC [8] which show a hump in G⁡(q)G(q) near 2​kF2k_{F} that is not present in previous parametrizations. This feature is included in the parametrization of Kaplan and Kukkonen [43], i.e., the intermediate term in Eq. (8). However, the amplitude of the hump is uncertain due to increasingly large error bars in the QMC data for q>2​kFq>2k_{F}. Our DMC data confirm the presence of such a feature, but we find the enhancement to be quite small. Moreover, our significantly smaller error bars (obtained using a backflow transformation for q>1.75​kFq>1.75k_{F} and rs=2r_{s}=2 to reduce the variance) resolve the discrepancy between DMC and diagrammatic QMC reported in Ref. [8], as both methods now agree within error bars. Our DMC results, combined with the diagrammatic QMC data, therefore allow us to determine the parameters of Kaplan and Kukkonen more precisely (Sec. II.4).

With the smaller error bars, the large-wave-vector regime becomes reliably accessible. Starting from rs=5r_{s}=5, we find that G⁡(q)G(q) exhibits a softening above 2​kF2k_{F} and deviates from the monotonic behavior fitted by the existing parametrizations, before approaching the high-qq limit. This is because the intermediate-qq regime was essentially unexplored by previous DMC data (e.g., at the lowest density, rs=10r_{s}=10, the data of Moroni et al., shown as red squares in Fig. 6(f), do not extend beyond q≃3​kFq\simeq 3k_{F}, but the feature is discernible in their data as well), so the parametrizations of Moroni et al. and Corradini et al. were designed as smooth crossovers between the known low- and high-qq limits 11 1 In fact, the same behavior is also reported in Ref. [37], where the authors report the unpublished rs=100r_{s}=100 data of Moroni et al. for a fully polarized gas.. Our parametrization, designed to capture the nonmonotonic behavior of G⁡(q)G(q) in the intermediate-qq region, accurately reproduces the DMC data throughout the whole range.

This feature is a precursor of a more pronounced nonmonotonicity due to growing exchange-correlation effects, as we show in Fig. 7 at rs=20,30,50r_{s}=20,30,50. At stronger coupling, we see that G⁡(q)G(q) develops a clear structure that gives rise to a local minimum. In contrast to the existing parametrization proposed by Corradini et al. (dash-dotted line, which is an extrapolation in this density range) that assumed monotonic behavior, the amplitude of this structure grows systematically with rsr_{s} and G⁡(q)G(q) approaches 11 at its local minimum. The position of the minimum shifts only slightly with density, moving from q≃3.3​kFq\simeq 3.3k_{F} to 3.2​kF3.2k_{F} as rsr_{s} increases. The suppression toward G⁡(q)≃1G(q)\simeq 1 implies that the response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) tends toward the noninteracting response around the same qq-value. This is an interesting feature, since it implies that the effective interaction vc​(q)​[1−G⁡(q)]v_{c}(q)[1-G(q)] between electrons nearly vanishes (see Eq. (3)). The exchange-correlation effects cancel the Coulomb interaction, and the gas responds to a perturbation of this wave vector like a noninteracting system despite being strongly correlated. Our parametrization (Sec. II.4) is constructed to capture this nonmonotonic behavior. Similar observations in the Bose liquid, the one-component plasma, and the 2D electron gas have been reported in the literature, with various possibilities attributed to strong liquid [63] or Coulomb interaction [64], scattering of electron pairs of opposite spin [65], the 2​kF2k_{F}-singularity in the response function responsible for Friedel oscillations [37], etc. In our companion paper [46], as well as in Sec. III.2, we show how this feature in G⁡(q)G(q) relates to short-range order in the electron liquid as it approaches the Wigner crystallization transition.

Beyond the local minimum, we see in Fig. 7 that G⁡(q)G(q) approaches its large-qq limit. Whether it does so with further, smaller oscillations cannot be resolved with our current data. Similar nonmonotonic structure in G⁡(q)G(q) has been reported in PIMC calculations [34, 33], but whether it is a ground-state property or a finite-temperature effect has remained an open question, since the fermion sign problem prevents PIMC from reaching low temperatures [66, 35]. Therefore, for the high-rsr_{s} panels of Fig. 7, we also show the finite-temperature PIMC results of Ref. [34] for Θ=0.5\Theta=0.5, which allow a direct comparison between ground-state and finite-temperature results. As panels (d)–(f) show, the PIMC data are in quantitative agreement with our T=0T=0 results, demonstrating that this structure is inherited from the ground state of the strongly coupled electron liquid rather than being a thermal effect.22 2 At rs=100r_{s}=100 (not shown), close to Wigner crystallization, the PIMC data for G⁡(q)G(q) no longer agree quantitatively, although the same structure is present.. Moreover, via Eq. (3), the agreement in G⁡(q)G(q) implies that the thermal changes in χ−1​(q)\chi^{-1}(q) and χ0−1​(q)\chi_{0}^{-1}(q) largely cancel, i.e., that the temperature dependence of χ⁡(q)\chi(q) at Θ=0.5\Theta=0.5 is carried predominantly by χ0​(q)\chi_{0}(q). This is consistent with panels (a)–(c) of Fig. 7, where χ⁡(q)\chi(q) itself, in which no such cancellation occurs, agrees less well between PIMC and DMC. This suggests that G⁡(q)G(q) determined at moderate temperatures can be used to obtain χ⁡(q)\chi(q) at T→0T\to 0, and vice versa.

Finally, we show in Fig. 8 the results for rs=100r_{s}=100, the lowest density we consider. The inset shows the ratio χ​(q)/χ0​(q)\chi(q)/\chi_{0}(q). At such low density, whether the ground state of the electron gas is liquid or crystalline is still not precisely known, and our data show interesting features that could be related to the onset of such a transition. First, we see that the suppression of χ⁡(q)\chi(q) toward the noninteracting response (dashed gray line) is the strongest among all densities considered, with χ⁡(qmin)/χ0​(qmin)=1.00±0.02\chi(q_{\mathrm{min}})/\chi_{0}(q_{\mathrm{min}})=1.00\pm 0.02 at q≃3.2​kFq\simeq 3.2k_{F} (see inset). Second, we also see a secondary peak in χ/χ0\chi/\chi_{0} at about twice the wave vector of the first peak, which leaves a direct imprint on the excitation spectrum of the electron liquid [46].

III.2 Relation to short-range order

The structure in G⁡(q)G(q) emerges in the same range of rsr_{s} in which g⁡(r)g(r) and S⁡(q)S(q) develop pronounced correlation features, suggesting that the two are related. Here, we show that the feature in G⁡(q)G(q) is a manifestation of the same physical phenomenon that shapes g⁡(r)g(r) and S⁡(q)S(q), commonly referred to as short-range order.

Electron liquid with short-range order

Before turning to our analysis, we characterize how the electron liquid evolves as the coupling increases until it eventually crystallizes into a bcc Wigner crystal at rs≃87r_{s}\simeq 87–113113 [56, 48, 57, 58]. Figure 9 shows the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r) from weak coupling up to near crystallization (rs=90r_{s}=90), obtained from separate DMC simulations of the unperturbed electron gas with a liquid trial wave function. For comparison, we also show g⁡(r)g(r) of the bcc Wigner crystal at rs=110r_{s}=110 (solid black line), taken from the DMC calculations of Ref. [57]. As the coupling increases, a peak develops in g⁡(r)g(r) and becomes pronounced for rs≳20r_{s}\gtrsim 20. The location of this peak is r≃3.3/kFr\simeq 3.3/k_{F}, which corresponds to the typical separation between an electron and its nearest neighbors. Interestingly, this peak coincides with the nearest-neighbor distance in the bcc Wigner crystal, rnn=3.38/kFr_{\mathrm{nn}}=3.38/k_{F} 33 3 The height of this peak increases with rsr_{s} and then saturates, with the rs=80r_{s}=80 and 9090 curves almost on top of each other, i.e., the local order saturates before long-range order sets in.. While the oscillations of g⁡(r)g(r) decay in the liquid, they persist to long range in the crystal phase.

The emergence of such a peak at the nearest-neighbor distance has been identified as short-range order in the literature [69, 70], and indicates that the liquid is approaching the Wigner crystallization transition [71, 72]. Apart from the peak and oscillations of g⁡(r)g(r), short-range order also shows up in the steepness of g⁡(r)g(r) on its rising edge, around kF​r=2k_{F}r=2, close to the radius of the sphere available to each electron, i.e., the Wigner–Seitz radius rs≃1.92/kFr_{s}\simeq 1.92/k_{F}. Compared with the weakly coupled liquid at rs=5r_{s}=5, g⁡(r)g(r) drops much more steeply toward r→0r\to 0 when short-range order is present. This depletion is more easily seen in the xc hole, n0​[g​(r)−1]n_{0}[g(r)-1], which measures the depletion of electrons around a reference electron [73, 3]. The inset of Fig. 9 shows the xc hole as a two-dimensional cut through the reference electron for rs=5r_{s}=5 and rs=90r_{s}=90. The liquid with short-range order has a noticeably more localized xc hole than the weakly coupled liquid. This can be quantified by the fraction of the missing electron within the Wigner–Seitz radius, −n0∫0rs[g(r)−1] 4πr2dr-n_{0}\int_{0}^{r_{s}}[g(r)-1]\,4\pi r^{2}\,dr, which would equal unity for a completely empty Wigner–Seitz sphere. This fraction grows from 57%57\% at rs=5r_{s}=5 to 95%95\% at rs=90r_{s}=90 (98%98\% in the crystal). The localized xc hole and the nearest-neighbor peak thus appear together, suggesting that both are signatures of short-range order: the region around each electron is nearly depleted up to its Wigner–Seitz radius, while its neighbors accumulate at the nearest-neighbor distance, reminiscent of the local structure of the bcc Wigner crystal.

In reciprocal space, short-range order mainly corresponds to a peak in the static structure factor S⁡(q)S(q), arising from the oscillations in g⁡(r)g(r), followed by further oscillations, arising from the steepness of the xc hole, that are damped out at large wave vectors. Just as for g⁡(r)g(r), this peak in S⁡(q)S(q) coincides with the first Bragg peak of the incipient Wigner crystal, located at q≃2.28​kFq\simeq 2.28k_{F}. The location of the peak therefore tracks the evolution from short-range order in the liquid to long-range order in the crystal. In the following, we relate these signatures of short-range order, the nearest-neighbor peak in g⁡(r)g(r) and S⁡(q)S(q) and the steepness of the xc hole, to the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q).

Calculations of S⁡(q)S(q) and g⁡(r)g(r) from G⁡(q)G(q)

The static structure factor S⁡(q)S(q) can be obtained directly from DMC. Alternatively, it follows from linear response theory via S(q)=−1π​n0∫0∞Imχ(q,ω)dωS(q)=-\frac{1}{\pi n_{0}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{Im}\,\chi(q,\omega)\,d\omega, which, however, requires the dynamic density response function χ⁡(q,ω)\chi(q,\omega). The latter is determined by the dynamic local field factor G⁡(q,ω)G(q,\omega), the frequency-dependent generalization of G⁡(q)G(q). Here, we use the adiabatic (static) approximation G⁡(q,ω)≈G⁡(q)G(q,\omega)\approx G(q), which is exact at ω=0\omega=0 and neglects the frequency dependence. Our parametrization of G⁡(q)G(q) then yields χ⁡(q,ω)\chi(q,\omega) via the Dyson equation,

χ⁡(q,ω)=χ0​(q,ω)1−vc​(q)​[1−G⁡(q)]​χ0​(q,ω),\chi(q,\omega)=\frac{\chi_{0}(q,\omega)}{1-v_{c}(q)[1-G(q)]\chi_{0}(q,\omega)}, (10)

where χ0​(q,ω)\chi_{0}(q,\omega) is the noninteracting density response function [3]. From here, one can obtain the dynamic structure factor as S⁡(q,ω)=−1π​n0​Im​χ​(q,ω)S(q,\omega)=-\frac{1}{\pi n_{0}}\mathrm{Im}\chi(q,\omega).

Figures 10 and 11 show the static structure factor S⁡(q)S(q) and the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r) obtained from DMC calculations (circles, calculated independently from the unperturbed gas) and from the adiabatic approximation (lines) using Eq. (10) for rs=20,30,50,80,90r_{s}=20,30,50,80,90. Since our goal is to investigate the effect of the feature in G⁡(q)G(q) on S⁡(q)S(q), we also show the case where G⁡(q)G(q) is featureless for comparison, i.e., the parametrization of Corradini et al. (dash-dotted lines). In all cases, g⁡(r)g(r) is obtained from the corresponding S⁡(q)S(q) by Fourier transform. Since the adiabatic approximation neglects the frequency dependence of G⁡(q,ω)G(q,\omega), the resulting large-qq behavior of S⁡(q)S(q) is incorrect, and the corresponding small-rr behavior of g⁡(r)g(r) is unreliable (gray curves in Fig. 11). In the DMC data, a peak develops in S⁡(q)S(q) near q≃2.2​kFq\simeq 2.2k_{F} as the liquid becomes more strongly coupled. As correlations grow, the peak becomes more pronounced and is followed by a dip, consistent with the short-range order discussed above.

The solid curves in Fig. 10 show that the effect of the feature in the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) is twofold. First, it reproduces the dip in S⁡(q)S(q) after the main peak as rsr_{s} increases, which a featureless G⁡(q)G(q) completely misses (red arrows). The equivalent picture in real space is shown in Fig. 11, where the red arrows mark the corresponding suppression of g⁡(r)g(r) on its rising edge, at kF​r≃2.24k_{F}r\simeq 2.24, due to the feature in G⁡(q)G(q). Since this suppression is tied to the localization of the xc hole (Fig. 9), the feature in G⁡(q)G(q) is a signature of short-range order in the electron liquid. Consistently, the real-space xc kernel fxc​(r)f_{\mathrm{xc}}(r), i.e., the Fourier transform of −vc​(q)​G​(q)-v_{c}(q)G(q), has a sharp positive peak at kF​r≃2.2k_{F}r\simeq 2.2, on the rising edge of the xc hole (dashed circles in the inset of Fig. 9), at the same distance as the red arrows in Fig. 11. This peak implies that density modulations cost exchange-correlation energy at this distance. Both this peak and the suppression marked by the red arrows disappear when the feature is removed from G⁡(q)G(q). For details, see the companion paper [46].

Second, the feature also reproduces the correct location of the main peak in S⁡(q)S(q). Without it, the main peak position is overestimated at all densities, which in real space (Fig. 11) corresponds to an underestimation of the typical separation between an electron and its nearest neighbors (black arrows in Figs. 10 and 11). These observations indicate that the features in S⁡(q)S(q), g⁡(r)g(r), and G⁡(q)G(q) are related and emerge together with short-range order. This is consistent with studies of the strongly coupled one-component plasma, the classical analog of our system, where the relation between G⁡(q)G(q) and S⁡(q)S(q) is well established [74]. Although the adiabatic approximation is quantitatively inaccurate at large qq and small rr, as discussed above, the qualitative agreement with DMC is clear. The same agreement also holds for other approximations, such as the single-mode approximation (SMA), in which the dynamic structure factor is approximated by a single sharp collective mode, S⁡(q,ω)≈S⁡(q)​δ​(ω−ωq)S(q,\omega)\approx S(q)\delta(\omega-\omega_{q}) [46].

IV Conclusions and Outlook

We have presented diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) and the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) of the three-dimensional electron gas at zero temperature. Our results extend the zero-temperature QMC data beyond the metallic regime and across the liquid phase up to the vicinity of Wigner crystallization. These calculations were made possible by a careful analysis and control of the systematic errors that arise in the strongly coupled regime. First, we established a semi-empirical scaling of the linear-response window with density, which guides the choice of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}. Second, we demonstrated that a backflow transformation, while lowering the energy substantially, leaves the extracted χ⁡(q)\chi(q) unchanged, so that Slater–Jastrow trial wave functions suffice for the response. Third, we showed that the scaling α\alpha of the perturbing potential entering the Slater determinant must be optimized, since a poor choice alters the curvature of E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) and can even reverse its sign and thereby lead to an unphysical response. We provided a closed-form expression for the optimal α⁡(q,rs)\alpha(q,r_{s}), valid for 2≤rs≤1002\leq r_{s}\leq 100, which removes the need for a separate optimization in future calculations.

Finally, we showed that the local field factor remains insensitive to system size even at very large rsr_{s} values wherever our data resolve it, and that the correction based on the noninteracting response alone removes the dominant finite-size error in χ⁡(q)\chi(q). The time step was chosen small enough to ensure that the time-step bias is negligible. Together, these results show that the strongly coupled regime can be treated with standard Slater–Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes, paving the way for future calculations of the response of the electron gas and related systems.

At metallic densities, our results agree with previous DMC data and parametrizations, extend them to q<kFq<k_{F}, where they are consistent with the compressibility sum rule, and resolve the discrepancy between DMC and diagrammatic QMC at intermediate wave vectors. Beyond this regime, G⁡(q)G(q) develops a pronounced nonmonotonic structure at intermediate wave vectors, already discernible at rs=5r_{s}=5, whose amplitude grows with rsr_{s} and which is absent from all existing parametrizations. The quantitative agreement with finite-temperature PIMC data at rs=20r_{s}=20–5050 establishes this feature as a ground-state property of the electron liquid. Finally, we have shown that the inclusion of this feature in G⁡(q)G(q) reproduces the correct physical behaviors of the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r) and the static structure factor S⁡(q)S(q), which are missed by a featureless G⁡(q)G(q), and that this feature is related to the emergence of short-range order in the electron liquid, as seen in the calculations of g⁡(r)g(r) and S⁡(q)S(q).

The parametrization of G⁡(q)G(q) used throughout this work, given in the companion paper [46], reproduces our data over the full liquid phase and is directly usable for numerous applications. For instance, it can be used to construct exchange-correlation functionals in time-dependent density functional theory [75, 76, 77], which is widely used for electronic structure calculations of materials. It can also be used to describe dynamical and spectral properties in the electron gas [9, 78] and in real materials [9, 40, 79, 80, 81, 82], to construct effective electron–electron interactions [7, 83, 84], and to extend response calculations of warm dense matter to lower temperatures [35], where current PIMC calculations are limited by the fermion sign problem. Additionally, our results can serve as benchmarks for future theoretical and computational studies of the electron gas and related systems.

The methodology developed here is not specific to the density response of the unpolarized three-dimensional gas. In fact, it can be applied directly to the spin response, through a spin-dependent perturbation, to partially polarized systems, and to the two-dimensional electron gas, where crystallization occurs at much higher density and where the interplay between charge and spin correlations at intermediate wave vectors remains to be established.

Data Availability

The data that support the findings of this study, i.e., the local field factor G⁡(q)G(q) from which the static density response function χ⁡(q)\chi(q) can be obtained, the static structure factor S⁡(q)S(q), and the pair correlation function g⁡(r)g(r), are openly available in the Zenodo repository [85].

We use Hartree atomic units, kF=(9​π/4)1/3/rsk_{F}=(9\pi/4)^{1/3}/r_{s} and n0=3/(4​π​rs3)n_{0}=3/(4\pi r_{s}^{3}). The local field factor satisfies

G⁡(q)→q→0A​(qkF)2,G⁡(q)→q→∞C​(qkF)2+B.G(q)\xrightarrow{q\to 0}A\left(\frac{q}{k_{F}}\right)^{2},\qquad G(q)\xrightarrow{q\to\infty}C\left(\frac{q}{k_{F}}\right)^{2}+B. (11)

The coefficient AA follows from the compressibility sum rule [32, 37],

A⁡(rs)=14−kF24​π​d​μcd​n=14−(9​π/4)2/3​rs227​(rs​ϵc′′−2​ϵc′),\begin{split}A(r_{s})&=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{k_{F}^{2}}{4\pi}\frac{d\mu_{c}}{dn}\\ &=\frac{1}{4}-\frac{(9\pi/4)^{2/3}\,r_{s}^{2}}{27}\left(r_{s}\,\epsilon_{c}^{\prime\prime}-2\,\epsilon_{c}^{\prime}\right),\end{split} (12)

where μc=d⁡(n​ϵc)/d​n\mu_{c}=d(n\epsilon_{c})/dn, primes denote derivatives with respect to rsr_{s}, and the exchange contribution is the constant 1/41/4.

The coefficient CC is set by the correlation contribution to the kinetic energy [25, 32],

C⁡(rs)=−π2​kF​d⁡(rs​ϵc)d​rs=π2​kF​tc,C(r_{s})=-\frac{\pi}{2k_{F}}\frac{d(r_{s}\epsilon_{c})}{dr_{s}}=\frac{\pi}{2k_{F}}\,t_{c}, (13)

where tc=−ϵc−rs​ϵc′t_{c}=-\epsilon_{c}-r_{s}\epsilon_{c}^{\prime} is the correlation kinetic energy per electron given by the virial theorem.

For the correlation energy per electron ϵc​(rs)\epsilon_{c}(r_{s}) we use the Perdew–Wang parametrization [86] of the unpolarized gas,

ϵc​(rs)=−2​a0PW​(1+α1PW​rs)​ln⁡(1+1D),\epsilon_{c}(r_{s})=-2a_{0}^{\mathrm{PW}}(1+\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{PW}}r_{s})\ln\!\left(1+\frac{1}{D}\right), (14)

where D=2​a0PW​(β1​rs1/2+β2​rs+β3​rs3/2+β4​rs2)D=2a_{0}^{\mathrm{PW}}\left(\beta_{1}r_{s}^{1/2}+\beta_{2}r_{s}+\beta_{3}r_{s}^{3/2}+\beta_{4}r_{s}^{2}\right), with a0PW=0.031091a_{0}^{\mathrm{PW}}=0.031091, α1PW=0.21370\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{PW}}=0.21370, β1=7.5957\beta_{1}=7.5957, β2=3.5876\beta_{2}=3.5876, β3=1.6382\beta_{3}=1.6382, and β4=0.49294\beta_{4}=0.49294. The same ϵc\epsilon_{c} enters both AA and CC, and we use it for every model of G⁡(q)G(q) shown in this work, including those of Refs. [32, 37]. Evaluating AA and CC with the Perdew–Zunger form [87] instead changes AA by less than 0.5%0.5\% and CC by 11–4%4\%. The resulting change in χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is below 0.3%0.3\% for rs≤20r_{s}\leq 20, and reaches about one statistical error bar at rs=90r_{s}=90.

The constant BB is taken from the parametrization of Ref. [32], which is based on the DMC calculations of Ref. [26],

B⁡(rs)=1+a1B​rs1/2+a2B​rs3/23+b1B​rs1/2+b2B​rs3/2,B(r_{s})=\frac{1+a_{1}^{B}r_{s}^{1/2}+a_{2}^{B}r_{s}^{3/2}}{3+b_{1}^{B}r_{s}^{1/2}+b_{2}^{B}r_{s}^{3/2}}, (15)

with a1B=2.15a_{1}^{B}=2.15, a2B=0.435a_{2}^{B}=0.435, b1B=1.57b_{1}^{B}=1.57, and b2B=0.409b_{2}^{B}=0.409. Equation (15) was fitted for rs≤10r_{s}\leq 10, so for rs>10r_{s}>10 it is an extrapolation, and is not analyzed in this work since the regime it affects is either not covered by our DMC data or the error bars are too large to be sensitive to it.

Appendix B Determining the perturbation range

In this appendix, we describe our procedure for selecting the range of perturbation amplitudes v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} used to fit the DMC energies E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) and extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q), which is crucial for obtaining reliable results. The main challenge is to select a range that is sufficiently small to remain in the linear-response regime, but sufficiently large to ensure a good signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the DMC energies. At small v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}, the energy shift E⁡(v𝐪)−E0∝v𝐪2E(v_{\mathbf{q}})-E_{0}\propto v_{\mathbf{q}}^{2} becomes comparable to the statistical error of the DMC energy, so the curvature is poorly determined, which leads to very large error bars in χ⁡(q)\chi(q). At large v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}, the higher-order terms in Eq. (2) become significant and bias the quadratic coefficient, and hence χ⁡(q)\chi(q). Since each amplitude requires an independent optimization and DMC calculation, a poorly chosen range is also costly. We have found that this range depends on both the density and the wave vector, and we have developed a systematic procedure to determine it. Over the densities considered here, the appropriate amplitudes span almost two orders of magnitude.

Figure 12 demonstrates our strategy for selecting the range of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} used to fit E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) and extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q), for a single density and wave vector. The main panel shows the DMC energies (symbols) with the quadratic fit of Eq. (2) (solid). As one can see, one needs to select a range of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} that is neither too small, where the SNR is low, nor too large, where the response is no longer linear. We indicate these two regions with hatched areas in the main panel. The lower panel shows the SNR (circles) and reduced χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} of the quadratic fit (triangles). The best extraction of χ⁡(q)\chi(q) is obtained in the linear-response regime, where the SNR is sufficiently high and the reduced χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} of the quadratic fit is sufficiently low. Beyond the linear regime, χν2\chi^{2}_{\nu} rises by one to three orders of magnitude within a few v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} points (see lower panel), so any threshold of order unity selects the same range. We have used the criteria of SNR >10>10 and χν2<5\chi^{2}_{\nu}<5 to select the range of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} used for the quadratic fit.

The demonstration in Fig. 12 is done for a single point. Selecting the valid range of v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}}, on the other hand, has a nontrivial dependence on both rsr_{s} and qq. As we have seen in Figs. 1(a) and 1(b), the linear-response regime shrinks significantly as one goes from rs=5r_{s}=5 to rs=70r_{s}=70. Determining this dependence by brute force is prohibitively expensive. For this, we have solved the noninteracting problem perturbed by the same cosine potential, and found that the maximum v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} allowed to remain in the quadratic regime scales as rs−pr_{s}^{-p} with p≃1.4p\simeq 1.4–1.51.5. Since we have found the interacting linear-response window to be smaller than the noninteracting one, we then determined the interacting v𝐪maxv_{\mathbf{q}}^{\mathrm{max}} at a single density (rs=5r_{s}=5), by sampling v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} between zero and the noninteracting maximum, and we transferred it to the other densities assuming the same rs−pr_{s}^{-p} scaling. In each case, E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) was verified to remain in the quadratic regime (by the criteria defined above). The resulting amplitudes are shown in the right panel of Fig. 12, together with the fit v𝐪max=0.1212​rs−1.43v_{\mathbf{q}}^{\mathrm{max}}=0.1212\,r_{s}^{-1.43} Ha, whose exponent is taken from the noninteracting problem and whose prefactor is fitted to the data points. This avoids scanning v𝐪v_{\mathbf{q}} at every density, and it provides a guide for choosing the perturbation amplitude in future calculations. Note that the window also depends on qq: around q∼2​kFq\sim 2k_{F}, the linear-response regime for higher rsr_{s} values is significantly smaller compared to other wave vectors, as shown by the dash-dotted lines in Figs. 1(a) and 1(b). We handle this by successively discarding the largest perturbation amplitude until the criteria defined above, i.e., SNR >10>10 and χν2<5\chi^{2}_{\nu}<5, hold. All results that we present in this work are obtained using this procedure and criteria.

Appendix C Effects of twist averaging on χ⁡(q)\chi(q)

Twist-averaged boundary conditions [88] are a common alternative to analytic corrections for one-body finite-size errors. We test them at rs=5r_{s}=5 for Ne=54N_{e}=54 with 𝐪=(3,0,0)​ 2​π/L\mathbf{q}=(3,0,0)\,2\pi/L and Ne=162N_{e}=162 with 𝐪=(3,2,2)​ 2​π/L\mathbf{q}=(3,2,2)\,2\pi/L. For each twist, drawn from a Halton sequence starting at Γ\Gamma, we perform DMC calculations at fixed NeN_{e} and at the production perturbation amplitudes, average E⁡(v𝐪)E(v_{\mathbf{q}}) over twists, and extract χ⁡(q)\chi(q) from its curvature. Figure 13 shows the result as a function of the number of twists, together with the Γ\Gamma-point value corrected with Eq. (6). With increasing NtwN_{\mathrm{tw}}, the twist average moves away from the uncorrected Γ\Gamma value (Ntw=1N_{\mathrm{tw}}=1) toward the corrected one, recovering most of the correction. For Ne=162N_{e}=162, −χ/n0-\chi/n_{0} goes from 10.8410.84 at Γ\Gamma to 11.48±0.1311.48\pm 0.13 after 32 twists, compared with 11.76±0.0511.76\pm 0.05 for the corrected Γ\Gamma value. For Ne=54N_{e}=54, the uncorrected Γ\Gamma value is already closer to the corrected one, and the twist average remains within 2​σ2\sigma of it for all Ntw≥2N_{\mathrm{tw}}\geq 2, reaching 12.64±0.1612.64\pm 0.16 after 96 twists, compared with 12.29±0.1612.29\pm 0.16. In both cases, the twist average agrees with the corrected Γ\Gamma value to within 2–3%, i.e., within about 2​σ2\sigma. The remaining difference is expected for fixed-NeN_{e} twist averaging. For a size-independent G⁡(q)G(q) [Fig. 3(a)], the twist dependence of χ⁡(q)\chi(q) enters only through the noninteracting response at each twist, so the procedure can reach the thermodynamic limit only if it recovers the Lindhard function for noninteracting electrons. At fixed NeN_{e} it does not, because each twist fills its own NeN_{e} lowest levels and the averaged Fermi sphere is distorted [88]. Fixing the chemical potential instead avoids this at the cost of a fluctuating particle number (grand-canonical twist averaging), which could in principle lead to a more accurate size correction but was not tested here. Throughout this work, we keep NeN_{e} fixed for all twists (canonical twist averaging) and use Eq. (6), which inserts the thermodynamic-limit χ0\chi_{0} directly from a single twist.
